extracted.intended_audience: students and practitioners of logic, philosophers/scientists interested in methods of induction and causal inquiry
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance on four inductive methods (Agreement, Difference, Concomitant Variations, Residues) and ancillary principles for establishing causation from observed phenomena; includes examples (theory of dew) and cautions (plurality of causes, intermixture of effects).

rubrics_metrics.name: Method of Agreement
rubrics_metrics.description: Identify a circumstance common to multiple diverse instances in which the same effect occurs and treat that common circumstance as a possible antecedent (cause or invariable concomitant).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The method suggests that a circumstance common to all instances may be either the cause or an effect of the same cause; it is vulnerable to plurality of causes and coincidence when only a few instances are compared. It acquires independent value only when instances are very numerous and sufficiently various; otherwise it should be used to suggest hypotheses to be tested by the Method of Difference or by deductive reasoning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Method of Difference
rubrics_metrics.description: Compare a positive instance (where the effect occurs) with a negative instance (where it does not) that agrees in all circumstances except one, to infer that the differing circumstance is either the cause or an indispensable part of the cause.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When properly applied (positive and negative instances differing only by one antecedent), this method yields rigorous induction and is largely immune to the complication of plurality of causes. Example: cooling a surface experimentally to determine the temperature at which dew begins to form (direct experiment as canon of Difference).

rubrics_metrics.name: Method of Concomitant Variations
rubrics_metrics.description: When the antecedent cannot be absolutely excluded or when all substances possess the quality to some degree, infer causation from a proportional relation: if variation in a circumstance corresponds to systematic variation in the effect, the circumstance is implicated as a cause (or connected with the cause).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use when the quality of interest is present in all cases to differing degrees (e.g., conductivity or radiative power). Establish a 'scale of intensity' by exposing diversified conditions and observing proportional changes in the effect (dew deposition proportional to resistance to heat/radiation). This method is often necessary when absolute exclusion is impossible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Method of Residues
rubrics_metrics.description: Estimate and subtract the effects of all known antecedents from the observed phenomena; the remaining residual phenomenon points to additional, hitherto unknown causes to be investigated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Powerful for detecting new causal factors across diverse fields (examples: residual perturbations in cometary motion as evidence of a resisting medium; copper plate damping a magnetic needle leading to discovery of new interactions; residuals in chemical analyses leading to new elements). Requires careful calculation/estimation of known causes so the residual is meaningful.

rubrics_metrics.name: Indirect (Joint) Method of Agreement and Difference
rubrics_metrics.description: Combine the Methods of Agreement and Difference (and Concomitant Variations as needed) to prepare and analyze data so that the sole differing quality between instances can be detected and attributed as cause.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustrated by the 'Theory of Dew' example: use Agreement and Concomitant Variations to prepare instances, then apply the Indirect Method of Difference to detect the single property differentiating dew-forming and non-dew-forming substances. This combined approach can reach high assurance even when single methods alone would be insufficient.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of negative or contrary cases
rubrics_metrics.description: Actively seek and record instances where the effect is not produced (negative cases) because such comparisons are the condition necessary for the Method of Difference to operate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Noting absence of the phenomenon (e.g., no dew on polished metals) is essential to isolate causal circumstances. Negative cases help reveal what must be different and thus what antecedent(s) to test or exclude.

rubrics_metrics.name: Vary the circumstances / diversify exposures
rubrics_metrics.description: Systematically vary the material conditions (e.g., substance, surface finish, texture) to reveal patterns and construct scales of intensity for the effect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expose polished versus rough surfaces, different textures and materials, etc., to see how dew deposition changes; such diversification is a practical way to implement Concomitant Variations and to prepare comparisons for the Method of Difference.

rubrics_metrics.name: Requirement for Method of Difference: all other circumstances equal except one
rubrics_metrics.description: For a conclusive application of the Method of Difference, the compared instances must agree in all circumstances except the single antecedent under test.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If multiple differences exist between instances, the method cannot single out which difference is causal. The text emphasizes ensuring that the only distinguishing circumstance is the candidate cause before attributing causation to it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scale of intensity / proportionality as evidence of causal relation
rubrics_metrics.description: Establish that the effect varies in some proportion to a candidate causal quality (e.g., more dew where bodies radiate heat more or conduct heat less).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Concomitant Variations yield 'scales of intensity' that support the inference that the quality (or something connected with it) is a cause assisting the effect. Use graded, comparative observations across varied states to demonstrate proportional relationships.

rubrics_metrics.name: Corroboration by deduction from known laws
rubrics_metrics.description: Strengthen inductive inferences by showing the effect follows deductively from established laws (e.g., laws of vapour and heat explain dew formation).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Deductive corroboration can (a) prove causation as well as coexistence, (b) account for exceptions (e.g., absence of dew in very dry air), and (c) render natural experiments more interpretable. Use when properties and laws of agents present are known and calculable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Direct experiment to prove causation
rubrics_metrics.description: Use controlled manipulation (e.g., cooling a surface) to produce or remove the effect and thereby directly demonstrate causal connection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Direct experiments implement the Method of Difference; even small-scale artificial experiments that reproduce the phenomenon provide strong grounds to generalize the causal relation (with due consideration of scale and context).

rubrics_metrics.name: Natural experiments (when Nature supplies an isolated change)
rubrics_metrics.description: Treat naturally occurring, rapid, and well-defined changes in antecedents (e.g., clouds clearing) as experiments that satisfy Method of Difference, while noting limitations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Natural experiments can corroborate causal claims (clear sky causing radiative cooling and dew) but may involve complex means humans cannot fully analyze, so they often serve best as corroboration alongside other methods rather than sole proof.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beware plurality of causes
rubrics_metrics.description: A given effect may arise from several independent causes in different instances, so a common antecedent across cases need not be the true cause.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This caveat undermines the Method of Agreement when few or insufficiently varied instances are used. To mitigate, either obtain diverse instances showing the same antecedent repeatedly or use the Method of Difference to isolate causes. Treat Agreement results as suggestions until confirmed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Intermixture of effects (homogeneity of effects) complicates analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: Different causes may produce homogeneous or partially overlapping effects, so effects may be 'intermixed' and lack clear boundaries attributable to single causes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize that causes can combine to produce portions of an effect, and that this increases difficulty of analysis. Methods must account for mixtures (e.g., by subtracting known effects—Method of Residues—or by designing experiments that parse contributions).

rubrics_metrics.name: Need for large number and variety of instances to rely upon Agreement
rubrics_metrics.description: Only when instances are 'indefinitely multiplied and varied' does the Method of Agreement gain strong independent probative value that an antecedent is the cause rather than coincidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Repeated observation of the same antecedent across widely different contexts strengthens the presumption that it is causal; nevertheless, the investigator should still seek Difference-style tests or deductive explanations for final assurance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Logical conditions for asserting an ulterior (inherent) distinction via residues
rubrics_metrics.description: To claim an inherent or original distinction (e.g., mental superiority in a group) by Residues, one must subtract all differences explainable by known physical or circumstantial causes; what remains is the residual phenomenon indicating an ulterior cause.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Strong logical rigor is required: all known causal contributions must be estimated and removed; failure to do so undermines claims based on residuals. The text criticizes advocates who neglect establishing these necessary logical conditions.
